Part I. Posted on November 13, 2026 by Alan Weissberger Introduction: Today’s Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) nationwide U.S. flight departure halt, attributed to an unspecified “telecommunications problem,” Microsoft’s global cloud disruption yesterday, and other prolonged telecommunications outages highlight serious questions about the resilience of critical network infrastructure, the effectiveness of automatic failover and service restoration, and the adequacy of disaster-recovery capabilities. These incidents involved different systems and should not be assumed to share a common technical cause. However, both illustrate the consequences when essential network services become unavailable and recovery is neither immediate nor seamless. FAA – Telecommunications Failure Disrupts the U.S. National Airspace System: On November 13, 2026, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop for all departing flights following a telecommunications outage affecting air traffic control operations. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the communications issue was impacting all 22 U.S. Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs) , and FAA technicians were investigating. The FAA’s preliminary statement described the problem as a temporary telecommunications outage and said the ground stop was imposed for safety reasons. The 22 ARTCCs are a critical part of the U.S. National Airspace System. Unlike airport control towers, which manage aircraft movements on runways and in the immediate vicinity of airports, ARTCCs manage aircraft during the en route portion of their flights, primarily at higher altitudes between airports. They coordinate aircraft separation, traffic flows, handoffs between control sectors and the safe movement of aircraft through the national airspace system. A communications failure affecting these centers can have consequences well beyond the geographic location where the original problem occurred. ARTCCs depend on reliable communications with aircraft, other control facilities and supporting systems to manage traffic safely. If controllers cannot reliably communicate with aircraft or coordinate traffic handoffs, the FAA may have to reduce traffic volumes or suspend departures to maintain safe operating conditions. The disruption was substantial. According to FlightAware, more than 1,000 flights were canceled and nearly 10,000 delayed. Reuters reported that 4,042 flights were airborne and destined for U.S. airports when the FAA issued the ground stop. The disruption also affected international operations, forcing cancellations of some flights originating in Canada and Europe. FAA Flight Control Center ………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………….. The nationwide ground stop prevented additional aircraft from departing while the FAA investigated the problem and worked to restore communications. Thousands of aircraft already airborne were allowed to land, while flights still on the ground could not take off. Inbound international flights were to be handled on a case-by-case basis. The FAA was not ordering aircraft already in the air to land immediately; rather, it was restricting new departures to avoid adding traffic to an airspace system experiencing serious communications problems. The FAA’s action was only the second nationwide ground stop of departing flights since the September 11, 2001 attacks. The previous occurrence was in January 2023, when the FAA halted domestic departures for less than two hours following a failure of its NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system. That incident involved a different system and failure scenario and should not be confused with the November 2026 telecommunications outage. The Critical Question: Why Didn’t Redundancy Prevent a Nationwide Disruption? The central engineering issue is not simply why the telecommunications system failed, but why the failure resulted in a nationwide ground stop. The incident raises several important questions: What telecommunications infrastructure and services were affected, and how did the problem propagate across the ARTCC network? Were independent primary and alternate communications routes available to the affected centers? Did the outage involve a common network, switching facility, software platform, power source or other shared dependency? What backup communications systems and failover procedures were in place, and why were they unable to maintain sufficient service to avoid a nationwide suspension of departures? Were alternate facilities or operating procedures available to isolate the failure and maintain at least limited air traffic operations? These questions cannot be answered conclusively until the FAA provides a detailed technical explanation. As of the initial reports, the precise cause had not been established publicly. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication at that time of a malicious attack, while emphasizing that the cause remained under investigation. The possibility of a problem involving an update to the private communications network supporting FAA operations was raised in subsequent reporting, but should be treated as preliminary until confirmed by the FAA and its contractors. FAA Modernization: Acknowledged Problems, but Resilience Remains Essential The November 13 incident occurred as the FAA is undertaking a major modernization of its aging air traffic control infrastructure. The Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS) initiative includes replacing legacy telecommunications infrastructure, modernizing voice switches and radio systems, and upgrading other critical air traffic control technologies. A September 2026 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report, Air Traffic Control Systems: Ambitious New Modernization Effort Needs to Improve Cost and Schedule Planning (GAO-26-107992), describes both the scale of this effort and the challenges facing the FAA. By May 2026, the agency had replaced 2,560 of 5,170 aging copper communications wires with high-speed fiber-optic cables—approximately half of the planned replacements. The report also identifies significant cost-estimation and project-scheduling weaknesses that could delay modernization and prolong reliance on outdated systems. Modernization is clearly necessary, but replacing aging copper lines with fiber and upgrading equipment are not sufficient by themselves to guarantee network resilience. The architecture must also provide physically and logically diverse communications paths, independent backup facilities, automatic failover, effective fault isolation and tested disaster-recovery procedures. The FAA’s previously implemented backup arrangements for its NOTAM system should not be confused with backup communications for the ARTCC network. They address different systems and failure scenarios. The November 13 incident requires a separate examination of the communications architecture, route diversity, failover procedures and operational readiness supporting all 22 centers. Ultimately, the question is whether the FAA’s communications infrastructure was engineered to withstand the failure of individual links, facilities or shared network components—and, if so, why those protections were insufficient to prevent a nationwide ground stop. As of the initial reports, the precise technical cause had not been established publicly. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication at that time of a malicious attack, while emphasizing that the cause was still under investigation. Subsequent reporting raised the possibility of a problem involving an update to the private communications network supporting FAA operations, but that explanation should be treated as preliminary until confirmed by the FAA and its contractors. The FAA has been undertaking a major modernization of its aging air traffic control infrastructure, including replacing older copper communications lines with fiber and upgrading radio systems. The November 13 incident underscores why modernization must address not just equipment age and capacity, but also network architecture, physical and logical route diversity, automatic failover, fault isolation and disaster recovery. The FAA has been working to modernize aging air traffic control infrastructure. A September 2026 Government Accountability Office report, Air Traffic Control Systems: Ambitious New Modernization Effort Needs to Improve Cost and Schedule Planning (GAO-26-107992) , describes the scale of the modernization challenge and the risks of continued reliance on outdated systems. The FAA’s previously implemented backup arrangements for its NOTAM system should not be confused with backup communications for the regional air traffic control centers. They address different systems and failure scenarios. The November 13th incident requires a separate examination of communications architecture, route diversity, failover procedures and operational readiness. Microsoft: A Global Cloud-Service Disruption: A day earlier, on November 12, Microsoft experienced a widespread disruption affecting Microsoft 365 services, including Exchange Online, Outlook and other applications dependent on its cloud infrastructure. Microsoft reported that a significant number of servers had become unexpectedly unavailable. The remaining infrastructure experienced increased load, complicating recovery as affected servers were returned to service. The disruption continued across regions and affected businesses, government organizations and other customers. This raises a different but equally important question: how could a cloud platform operating at Microsoft’s scale lose enough server capacity to cause prolonged disruption across multiple services and regions? Cloud infrastructure is designed to distribute workloads across servers, availability zones and geographic regions. But distributing workloads does not automatically guarantee resilience. Shared software, configuration changes, dependencies, authentication services, traffic-management systems or common operational procedures can create failure domains that extend well beyond an individual server or data center. Microsoft’s incident also demonstrates that restoring infrastructure is not necessarily the same as restoring service. Recovery must account for traffic redistribution, overloaded surviving systems, dependency failures and the possibility that returning capacity to service may itself destabilize the environment. The Common Question: Where Was the Effective Backup? The FAA and Microsoft incidents are not evidence of the same underlying failure. They do, however, expose a common issue: the difference between having redundant infrastructure and maintaining uninterrupted service when something fails. A network may have multiple links, servers, data centers or geographic locations and still be vulnerable if those resources share a common failure point. Backup capacity is useful only if it is sufficiently independent, operationally available and capable of taking over under real-world failure conditions. ……………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………. Part II. 3 thoughts on “ Critical Network Outages: Why Isn’t Redundancy Working? Part I. ” Ken Pyle says: November 14, 2026 at 09:21 Great questions and overview, Alan. It sounds like the November 10th rollout of the SMART AI system was a coincidence and didn’t contribute to the outage. https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/icymi-us-transportation-secretary-sean-p-duffy-announces-lifting-nationwide-ground#:~:text=Secretary%20Duffy%20on%20the%20outdated%20air%20traffic,It's%20the%20old%20hardware%20that%20went%20down.%E2%80%9D https://www.flyingmag.com/faa-smart-ai-now-active-at-22-artccs-nationwide/ Regarding the upgrade, it sounds like they truly are using DS0s/T1s, which according to Gemini is the source of yesterday’s problem “Roughly a third of the FAA’s telecommunications network still relies on aging copper TDM leased lines—specifically T1 (1.544 Mbps) and DS0 (64 kbps) circuits—where individual timeslots are hard-pinned to critical air-to-ground radios and radar feeds. Because commercial carriers have largely retired their core TDM switches, these legacy copper “last-mile” lines now have to be translated into IP packets via fragile circuit emulation gateways across carrier fiber cores. When unexpected data bursts hit the tiny fixed-capacity buffers of these legacy TDM switches and routers—as happened during the November 13 outage—they overload and degrade data, which is why the FAA is racing to replace them with native Ethernet-over-fiber under its FENS modernization program.” Reply Alan Weissberger says: November 14, 2026 at 11:21 The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop on Friday evening at 8:15pm EST, November 13, 2026, after a roughly four-and-a-half-hour air traffic control communications disruption. Technical Root Cause & Redundancy Failure: • Legacy vs. Modern Equipment Overload: U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed the failure to a “data overload” where newly patched, modern equipment and software updates overwhelmed aging legacy telecommunications switches and routers within the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network managed by L3Harris Technologies. • Cascading Data Inconsistencies: The trouble reportedly originated around network routers at Chicago Midway International Airport before cascading across all 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers nationwide, generating conflicting and unstable radar/communications data. • Redundancy Limits: Rather than a clean failover to redundant backup paths, the legacy backbone degraded under the load of conflicting synchronized data packets—underscoring how simultaneous dual-vendor or mixed-generation patching can compromise high-availability safety-critical architectures. • Scale of Impact: More than 6,300 flights were canceled and 9,500 delayed according to FlightAware, with recovery expected to take days as airlines reposition crews and aircraft. Officials confirmed there was no indication of a cyberattack. Source: Google Gemini Reply Alan Weissberger says: November 14, 2026 at 11:42 From Google Gemini: Excellent two-part series dissecting why theoretical redundancy so often fails in production. Very timely analysis of both the FAA ground stop and the Microsoft 365 disruption. What stands out across both incidents is that control-plane and state-synchronization failures routinely bypass physical redundancy. In both cases, having backup links or geographically distributed servers did not prevent a wide-area outage because the failure mechanism—whether conflicting radar/routing packets cascading across the 22 ARTCCs or cascading load spikes as offline cloud servers rejoined the cluster—propagated through the very mechanisms meant to coordinate traffic. True fault isolation requires strict circuit-breaking and rate-limiting between failure domains so that a localized anomaly or recovery surge cannot destabilize healthy nodes. Following up on the root-cause updates regarding the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) outage: the Chicago Midway router overload highlights a critical blind spot in multi-year telecom modernization programs—mixed-generation transition risk. When legacy TDM/DS0 circuits are bridged into modern IP/MPLS or Ethernet-over-fiber cores via circuit emulation gateways, the timing, synchronization, and buffer characteristics of the two generations clash. Pushing modern software patches or synchronized routing bursts across legacy hardware with tiny fixed buffers doesn’t trigger a clean failover; instead, it induces common-mode congestion across both primary and backup paths simultaneously. Until legacy TDM dependencies are fully retired rather than merely emulated, “hybrid” redundancy remains a major single point of failure.
